| Date | May 25 – September 17, 1787 |
| Location | * [Pennsylvania State House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_House "Pennsylvania State House") (now Independence Hall) [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), Pennsylvania |

The **Constitutional Convention** took place in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") from May 25 to September 17, 1787.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJillson200931,_38-1) While the convention was initially intended to revise the league of states and the first system of [federal government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation"),[[2]](#cite_note-2) leading proponents of the Constitutional Convention, including [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison") of Virginia and [Alexander Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton") of New York, sought to create a new frame of government rather than revise the existing one.
The convention took place in Pennsylvania State House, later renamed [Independence Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Hall "Independence Hall"), in Philadelphia.

It was voted on by the delegates, inscribed on parchment by [Jacob Shallus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Shallus "Jacob Shallus") with engraving for printing, and [signed by 39 of 55 delegates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signing_of_the_United_States_Constitution "Signing of the United States Constitution") on September 17, 1787.

excerpts.text: And on May 25, twenty-four delegates — way less than a majority of the 74 selected — were present at Independence Hall.
Note the Arabic numerals identify the 39 delegates who signed the Constitution on September 17, 1787.

2) Or take the strange cases of George Clymer and Thomas Fitzsimons. What are we to make of the fact that Clymer and Fitzsimons of Pennsylvania spoke on August 21? Prior today, there are only two days of the Convention on which Clymer was clearly present. Over the remaining 22 days of the Convention, however, he was clearly present on eight of those days. Fitzsimons’s situation is just as curious. Prior today, there were only two days on which Fitzsimons was clearly present. Over the last 22 days of the Convention, he was clearly present on seven of those days. In other words he spoke or indicated as present. This coincides with the meeting of the Pennsylvania Assembly of which both Clymer and Fitzsimons were members. Or, take Robert Morris. There are only three days on which Robert Morris is clearly present: May 25 (the first day of the Convention), June 25, and September 17 (the last day of the Convention and the day of the signing of the Constitution.) How about the fact that there were only three clear days that Jared Ingersoll was present: May 26, June 25, and September 17. Thomas Mifflin is also difficult to track. He was clearly present on May 25, August 14, and September 17.

excerpts.text: On September 17, 1787, a group of men gathered in a closed meeting room to sign the greatest vision of human freedom in history, the U.S.
The Constitutional Convention started in May 1787 in Pennsylvania’s State House (which is now called Independence Hall).

On September 17, the group met one last time to conclude its business in Philadelphia, and to agree on how the Constitution would be sent to the Confederation Congress to start the ratification process with the states.
Of the 41 men in the room, 38 signed the document, with George Read also signing for an absent John Dickinson.
James McHenry, a Maryland delegate, also kept brief notes of what happened on September 17, 1787.

excerpts.text: Of the 70 delegates chosen as representatives to the [Constitutional Convention](https://www.britannica.com/event/Constitutional-Convention) of 1787, only 55 actually attended the proceedings in Philadelphia, and it is believed that there were never more than 46 of them in attendance at any one time. When it came time to affix their signatures to the soon-to-be famous parchment, 38 of the 41 delegates present became signatories. Citing objections that would become cornerstones for the [Anti-Federalists](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Anti-Federalists), [George Mason](https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-Mason), [Edmund Randolph](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edmund-Jennings-Randolph), and [Elbridge Gerry](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Elbridge-Gerry) refused to sign. [John Dickinson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Dickinson) could not attend the signing but authorized another delegate, George Read, to sign for him. So, in the end, there were 39 signers of the [U.S. Constitution](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Constitution-of-the-United-States-of-America).

**Constitutional Convention**, (1787), in U.S. history, convention that drew up the [Constitution of the United States](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Constitution-of-the-United-States-of-America). Stimulated by severe economic troubles, which produced radical political movements such as [Shays’s Rebellion](https://www.britannica.com/event/Shayss-Rebellion), and urged on by a demand for a stronger central government, the convention met in the Pennsylvania State House in [Philadelphia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Philadelphia) (May 25–September 17, 1787), ostensibly to [amend](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/amend) the Articles of [Confederation](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Articles-of-Confederation). All the states except [Rhode Island](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rhode-Island-state) responded to an invitation issued by the [Annapolis Convention](https://www.britannica.com/event/Annapolis-Convention) of 1786 to send delegates. Of the 74 deputies chosen by the state legislatures, only 55 took part in the proceedings; of these, 39 signed the [Constitution](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Constitution-of-the-United-States-of-America). The delegates included many of the leading figures of the period. Among them were [George Washington](https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-Washington), who was elected to preside, [James Madison](https://www.britannica.com/biography/James-Madison), [Benjamin Franklin](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Benjamin-Franklin), [James Wilson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/James-Wilson-United-States-statesman), [John Rutledge](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Rutledge), [Charles Pinckney](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-Pinckney), [Oliver Ellsworth](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Oliver-Ellsworth), and [Gouverneur Morris](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gouverneur-Morris).
